newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Refinery runs again at center of APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Refinery runs again at center of APIs.

text.p: REUTER SURVEY ESTIMATES* ACTUAL STOCKS FOR
FOR WEEK ENDED 05/30/97 WEEK ENDED 05/23/97-CHANGE
CRUDE...........UP 0.31 million bbls 316.120 UP 1.396 MLN
DISTILLATE......UP 2.00 million bbls 101.698 UP 3.319 MLN
GASOLINE........DN 0.50 MLN bbls 196.778 DN 1.119 MLN
UTILIZATION... UNCH/DN 0.13pct 96.7 DN 0.9 PCT
*NB - The survey estimate is derived by omitting the high and low forecast and averaging the rest.
(STOCKS IN THOUSANDS/BBLS, CHANGES IN MLN/BBLS)
Strong refinery utilization rates will once again take center stage in this week's American Petroleum Institute stocks data, with crude oil inventories seen showing little appreciable change.

Foreign crude imports are expected to have maintained a healthy pace in the last, but with refinery runs still hovering in the 96- to 97-percent range, inventory builds should be minimal, according to traders surveyed by Reuters.
And once again, with refinery margins improving slightly over the past week, the run-rate should weigh on any implied demand for gasoline, traders said.
"The higher utilization rates should wear on the whole complex over the next few weeks," said MPAS Inc President Bob MacMinn.

"The high level of crude imports should offset the record high crude runs, and higher yields are certainly outstripping demand on the distillate side. The runs will keep crude (prices) underpinned for now, but in the long run we'll just transfer that balance in crude to the products stocks, probably by the third quarter, which could get ugly," MacMinn said.
Crude oil stocks in the API data are expected to post, on average, a rise of about 313,000 barrels. Estimates ranged from a build of 2.5 million barrels to a draw of 2.5 to 3.0 million barrels.
MacMinn said the higher refinery run-rate "is going to have a negative impact on refining margins, and gas demand doesn't look like it's going to get much better."

Refco Inc analyst Victor Yu sees a similar scenario. "Crude stocks would be up despite the imports. I think seasonal gas demand should put a little dent in them, but with U.S. production at (current levels), we're not going to see much of a dent," Yu said.
William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co, is calling for a draw in crude stocks of about 3 million barrels.

"We had almost a 12-million-barrel build last year in this week, the week end May 31," he said, noting the effect of that week's build on year-over-year surplus, which currently stands at 18.3 million barrels, according to last week's API data.
"If there's any kind of draw this week, that surplus comparison may narrow a good bit. It strikes me that this week's data is going to be important," Brown said.
((--C. Thompson New York Energy Desk 212.859.1761))
